title: Scientists Burned Their Own Scrolls to Read Ancient Ones
summary: Imagine trying to read a book that's been turned into a lump of charcoal. That's the problem with over 1,800 scrolls from Herculaneum, an ancient Roman town buried by Mount Vesuvius in 79 C.E. The scrolls are too fragile to open — they'd crumble into dust. So scientists got creative. Douglas Seiler and his team made their own papyrus scrolls, wrote on them with ancient-style ink, and burned them. They even paid high school students to write passages from Star Wars and the Bible. Why? To test a new idea. If the ancient ink contained lead, that metal would absorb X-rays much more strongly than the burned papyrus. Then a computer could scan the scroll and reveal the writing without opening it. The experiment worked! Even tiny amounts of lead made the writing stand out. Lead absorbed up to 25 times more X-rays than the surrounding char. "With lead in the ink, you would get a huge friggin' signature," Seiler said. The team also found a cheap handheld scanner that can detect lead in a scroll. This could help find the best scrolls to read next. The Herculaneum library is the only intact library from ancient times. Reading it could uncover lost works of history, philosophy, and literature. "The stakes are the largest in the history of Greek literature," said one expert.
why_it_matters: This shows how a clever experiment — trying something out on a copy first — can solve a problem you can't risk testing on the real thing, just like practising a science project before the school fair.

background_read: Herculaneum was an ancient Roman town near the city of Naples in Italy, and it was buried when Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 C.E. — the same eruption that destroyed the town of Pompeii.
Papyrus (a paper-like material made from a tall river plant) was one of the main ways people wrote things down in the ancient Mediterranean world.
X-rays are the same invisible light doctors use to see the bones inside your body: heavy things like metal block them, while light, burnt materials let them pass through.
Article_Structure: WHO: Douglas Seiler and his team, who even paid high school students to write test passages, such as lines from Star Wars and the Bible.
WHAT: They burned their own papyrus scrolls written with ancient-style ink to test whether lead in the ink would let X-rays reveal writing inside a scroll without opening it.
WHERE: The real scrolls come from Herculaneum, an ancient Roman town buried by Mount Vesuvius in 79 C.E.
WHY: The Herculaneum library is the only intact library left from ancient times, so reading it could uncover lost works of history, philosophy and literature.

perspectives.description: They say the prize is huge, because the scrolls could bring back ancient books that no one has read for nearly 2,000 years.
They worry that any handling or scanning might damage the fragile, charred scrolls, so they want the safest possible methods used first.
Some people think time and money should go to today's problems, like schools and hospitals, rather than to burnt books from long ago.
